summary.text: Vapor pressure is the pressure of a vapor in balance with its liquid or solid form at a given temperature in a closed system.
It indicates a liquid's tendency to evaporate, and a substance with a high vapor pressure at normal temperatures is called volatile.
It increases with temperature, and a liquid's normal boiling point is the temperature where its vapor pressure equals the surrounding atmospheric pressure.

facts.label: Volatile
facts.value: High vapor pressure at normal temperatures

facts.label: Temperature trend
facts.value: Rises non-linearly as temperature goes up

facts.label: Units
facts.value: Measured in pressure units; the SI unit is the pascal

items.prompt: Liquid A's molecules cling to each other much more strongly than liquid B's do. Both sit at the same temperature. Which has the lower vapor pressure?

options.label: Liquid B, because loosely bound molecules hold together better
Neither, because temperature alone sets vapor pressure
Liquid A, because strongly bound molecules escape less readily
Liquid A, because strong attraction pushes molecules into the air

items.explain: Liquids with strong intermolecular interactions are likely to have smaller vapor pressures, and the reverse is true for weaker ones.

items.prompt: What must be true of a liquid for vapor bubbles to start forming in it at ordinary air pressure?

options.label: Its vapor pressure has reached the pressure of the surrounding air
It has absorbed a fixed amount of heat, whatever its temperature
Its surface tension has dropped to zero
The air above it has stopped moving

items.explain: The normal boiling point is the temperature at which the vapor pressure equals the ambient atmospheric pressure.

items.prompt: A sealed container holds a little liquid and its vapor. You warm it up. What happens to the vapor pressure?

options.label: It stays the same, because the container is sealed
It rises, but not in a straight-line pattern
It rises by the same amount for every degree
It falls, because the molecules are more spread out

items.explain: Vapor pressure increases with temperature, and non-linearly.

items.prompt: Two liquids sit in open dishes at room temperature. One has a lower boiling point than the other. Which has the higher vapor pressure?

options.label: The one that boils at the higher temperature
They match, because they are at the same room temperature
It is impossible to say without knowing the dish size
The one that boils at the lower temperature

items.explain: As a general trend, vapor pressures of liquids at ambient temperatures increase as boiling points decrease.

items.prompt: A mixture's vapor pressure comes out higher than the ideal formula (Raoult's law) predicts. What does this suggest about its molecules?

options.label: The attraction between them is weaker than in the pure liquids
The attraction between them is stronger than in the pure liquids
The mixture must contain charged particles that trap the vapor
The molecules are packed more tightly than in the pure liquids

items.explain: A higher-than-predicted vapor pressure suggests weaker attraction, so molecules are held in the liquid less strongly.

items.prompt: A lab tries to measure a vapor pressure below 1 kPa. How much can it trust the result?

options.label: Fully, because small pressures are the easiest to measure
Not much, because measurements that small are subject to major errors
Fully, as long as the liquid is heated first
Only if the liquid is replaced by a solid

items.explain: Measurement is simple between 1 and 200 kPa, but values below 1 kPa are subject to major errors.

paragraphs.heading: A vapor in balance
paragraphs.text: Picture a liquid sealed in a closed container at a fixed temperature. Particles leave the liquid and form a vapor above its surface, and in time the escaping particles and the vapor settle into a balance, called equilibrium. The pressure that this vapor then exerts is the vapor pressure. The same idea works for a solid sitting with its own vapor.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Vapor pressure shows how strongly a liquid tends to evaporate. A substance with a high vapor pressure at ordinary temperatures is called volatile. Exact values matter in medicine for inhaled anesthetics: most of them are liquids at body temperature, yet their vapor pressure is fairly high.

paragraphs.heading: Pull between molecules
paragraphs.text: Liquids whose molecules attract each other strongly tend to have low vapor pressures, and weak attraction gives high ones. Warming a liquid makes that attraction count for less against the draw of the gas phase, so the vapor pressure goes up. The rise is not a straight line, and it is often described by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation.

paragraphs.heading: What boiling really is
paragraphs.text: A liquid's normal boiling point is the temperature at which its vapor pressure equals the pressure of the air around it, defined as 1 atmosphere, 760 Torr or 101.325 kPa. Warm it a little past that point and the vapor can overcome the atmosphere, so bubbles of vapor form inside the liquid. Deeper in the liquid, bubbles need a slightly higher temperature, because the weight of fluid above adds pressure.

paragraphs.heading: An example: methyl chloride
paragraphs.text: As a general rule, liquids with lower boiling points have higher vapor pressures at room temperature. Methyl chloride shows this clearly on a chart comparing several liquids. At every temperature shown, its vapor pressure is the highest of the group. Its normal boiling point, −24.2 °C, is also the lowest of them.

paragraphs.heading: How it is measured
paragraphs.text: Vapor pressure is given in ordinary pressure units. The SI unit is the pascal, one newton per square meter, while medicine sometimes uses millimeters of mercury. Measuring it is simple for common pressures between 1 and 200 kPa. You purify the substance, seal it in a container, remove any foreign gas, and read the pressure of its vapor at different temperatures. Readings below 1 kPa carry large errors.
